text: Bleſſed is the man to whom the Lord imputeth not iniquitie, and in whoſe ſpirit there is no guile.
author: Tymme, Thomas, d. 1620.
title: The poore mans Pater noster with a preparatiue to praier: wherto are annexed diuers godly psalmes and meditations: collected out of the sacred scriptures, by Thomas Timme minister.

text: O Father which art in heuen, ye maker of all things, and moſte mightie Lorde, hear vs we beſéech thee which are héere troubled and turmoiled in earth, which are trauellers and pilgrimes therein, not onelie for a time, but for the moſt part, for a ſmall moment of time.
author: Tymme, Thomas, d. 1620.
title: The poore mans Pater noster with a preparatiue to praier: wherto are annexed diuers godly psalmes and meditations: collected out of the sacred scriptures, by Thomas Timme minister.

text: Howe dareſt thou (ſaith hee) miſerable man, preſume to come into the preſence of God with thy praiers? with what face canſt thou call him thy father, when as thou at no time haſt ſhewed thy ſelfe an obedient ſon?
author: Tymme, Thomas, d. 1620.
title: The poore mans Pater noster with a preparatiue to praier: wherto are annexed diuers godly psalmes and meditations: collected out of the sacred scriptures, by Thomas Timme minister.

text: We do not preſent our ſupplications before thee, for our owne righteouſnes, but for thy great tender mercies.
author: Tymme, Thomas, d. 1620.
title: The poore mans Pater noster with a preparatiue to praier: wherto are annexed diuers godly psalmes and meditations: collected out of the sacred scriptures, by Thomas Timme minister.

text: Then will they caſt vs in a pit & lay a ſtone of abſtinencie vppon vs, that we ſhall not ariſe againe.
author: Tymme, Thomas, d. 1620.
title: The poore mans Pater noster with a preparatiue to praier: wherto are annexed diuers godly psalmes and meditations: collected out of the sacred scriptures, by Thomas Timme minister.

text: Father I haue ſinned againſt heauen, & before thee, and am no more worthie to bee called thy ſon.
author: Tymme, Thomas, d. 1620.
title: The poore mans Pater noster with a preparatiue to praier: wherto are annexed diuers godly psalmes and meditations: collected out of the sacred scriptures, by Thomas Timme minister.

text: As the angels and ſaints doo thus reſt on thy will, O God alone, euen ſo other celeſtiall bodies alſo doo obeie the ſame.
author: Tymme, Thomas, d. 1620.
title: The poore mans Pater noster with a preparatiue to praier: wherto are annexed diuers godly psalmes and meditations: collected out of the sacred scriptures, by Thomas Timme minister.

text: Make vs to loue ſobrietie in our apparell, and temperance in all our meats and drinkes, that wee being in all our actions euermore directed and gouerned by thy good ſpirit, wee may glorifie thy holie name.
author: Tymme, Thomas, d. 1620.
title: The poore mans Pater noster with a preparatiue to praier: wherto are annexed diuers godly psalmes and meditations: collected out of the sacred scriptures, by Thomas Timme minister.

text: Let thy wrath, and anger, and heauie diſpleaſure bee turned from vs, which we haue deſerued, and take vs into thy fatherly fauour againe, that we may be thy ſonnes.
author: Tymme, Thomas, d. 1620.
title: The poore mans Pater noster with a preparatiue to praier: wherto are annexed diuers godly psalmes and meditations: collected out of the sacred scriptures, by Thomas Timme minister.

text: And Vologeſes to make preparations of warre with more aduantage, and ſuch as might match the Romans, or to remoue thoſe he ſuſpected as concurrents vnder the name of hoſtages; deliuereth the nobleſt of the Arſacides familie, whom Hostorius the Centurion ſent before by Vinidius for other occaſions receiued.
author: Tacitus, Cornelius.
title: The annales of Cornelius Tacitus. The description of Germanie

text: They fulfilling his commaundement, eſpieng a night when he had no guarde: with aide ſufficient, bound him, ſtopped his mouth, and drew him to the pallace.
author: Tacitus, Cornelius.
title: The annales of Cornelius Tacitus. The description of Germanie

text: Caeſar had further griefe the ſame yeere, partly by the death of one of Druſus children, and partly by the death of Lucillius Longus his friend, and partaker of all his fortunes, proſperous or aduerſe: and among the Senators, his only companion, when he withdrew himſelfe to Rhodes.
author: Tacitus, Cornelius.
title: The annales of Cornelius Tacitus. The description of Germanie

text: Domitius credit grew by his father, who was lord of the ſea in the ciuill wars; vntill he thruſt himſelf into Antonies faction; and after that into Caeſars.
author: Tacitus, Cornelius.
title: The annales of Cornelius Tacitus. The description of Germanie

text: But his brother ſurnamed Felix of late made gouernour of Iudaea, vſed not the ſame moderation; but bare himſelfe vpon his authoritie as a ſufficient warrant for all lewdnes whatſoeuer.
author: Tacitus, Cornelius.
title: The annales of Cornelius Tacitus. The description of Germanie

text: Beſides his counſell he ſtroke them into a feare, droue the Megiſtanas Armenians which firſt reuolted, out of their houſes: battered downe their caſtles; filled with like feare the plaines; the hils; the ſtrong and weake.
author: Tacitus, Cornelius.
title: The annales of Cornelius Tacitus. The description of Germanie

text: He began therefore to inueigh againſt her obſtinacie, and ſtirre Augusta hating her of olde, againſt her; and incenſed Liuia with the memorie of her late fact; ſuggeſting that her pride; bearing it ſelfe vppon her fruitfulnes in children, by the fauour of the people gaped after the ſoueraigntie.
author: Tacitus, Cornelius.
title: The annales of Cornelius Tacitus. The description of Germanie

text: Then word was brought Claudius as he was a banquetting, that Meſſallina was dead, not telling him whether by her owne hand, or any mans elſe: neither did he aske ſo much; but called for the cup, and went forward as he was woont to do at his banket.
author: Tacitus, Cornelius.
title: The annales of Cornelius Tacitus. The description of Germanie

text: As they haſtned to finiſh the worke, Blaeſus came in among them, rebuking ſome, and hindering now one, now another, and crying alowde, In my bloud rather embrue your hands; for it is a leſſer offence to ſlay the Lieutenant, then fall from the obedience of the Emperour.
author: Tacitus, Cornelius.
title: The annales of Cornelius Tacitus. The description of Germanie

text: The quene and Magistrates, in place of thy son Iesus Christ, woulde place their abhominable idol of bread: in place of our prest, after the order of Melchisedecke, they would place preestes after the order of Baal & Antichrist.
author: Bale, John, 1495-1563, attributed name.
title: An excellent and a right learned meditacion, compiled in two prayers most frutefull and necessary to be vsed and said of al ttue [sic] English men, in these daungerous daies of affliction, for the com

text: Let not the vncircumcised papists & carnal epicures triumphe ouer vs. Let them not giest vpon vs, with mockes & tauntes, in rimes and balades for their pastime, & say: wher is now their God? where is their christ? wher is their gospel? wher it their safegarde?
author: Bale, John, 1495-1563, attributed name.
title: An excellent and a right learned meditacion, compiled in two prayers most frutefull and necessary to be vsed and said of al ttue [sic] English men, in these daungerous daies of affliction, for the com

text: For this word which we preach, beleue and confesse, is not our worde, but thy word, not our expositions or cōstruinges, but the expositions and construinges of thy holye Spirite.
author: Bale, John, 1495-1563, attributed name.
title: An excellent and a right learned meditacion, compiled in two prayers most frutefull and necessary to be vsed and said of al ttue [sic] English men, in these daungerous daies of affliction, for the com

text: Suffer not the swynish sorte of Sodomites, to treade in the myre that precious pearle the gospell of thy glory, the only schole and learning of our saluation.
author: Bale, John, 1495-1563, attributed name.
title: An excellent and a right learned meditacion, compiled in two prayers most frutefull and necessary to be vsed and said of al ttue [sic] English men, in these daungerous daies of affliction, for the com

text: O lord, which art the helth, & help of al that faithfulli trust in the, deliuer vs in the multitude of thi mercies, frō the multitude of our sinnes, & from these deserued plages.
author: Bale, John, 1495-1563, attributed name.
title: An excellent and a right learned meditacion, compiled in two prayers most frutefull and necessary to be vsed and said of al ttue [sic] English men, in these daungerous daies of affliction, for the com

text: In steede of Christes sacrifyce, they wold thrust out vnto vs, an horrible sacriledge, and spoylyng thy sonne Iesus Christ of his glory.
author: Bale, John, 1495-1563, attributed name.
title: An excellent and a right learned meditacion, compiled in two prayers most frutefull and necessary to be vsed and said of al ttue [sic] English men, in these daungerous daies of affliction, for the com

text: Deliuer vs not (O heauenlye father) into the handes of the wicked, least their handle vs after their owne lust.
author: Bale, John, 1495-1563, attributed name.
title: An excellent and a right learned meditacion, compiled in two prayers most frutefull and necessary to be vsed and said of al ttue [sic] English men, in these daungerous daies of affliction, for the com

text: O Lord, suffer not these proude Philistines, to stoppe vp thy swete springes of lyuīg water, & instede therof to make vs drink perforce, of their stincking puddles of abhominable popyshe masses & mens imagined traditiōs.
author: Bale, John, 1495-1563, attributed name.
title: An excellent and a right learned meditacion, compiled in two prayers most frutefull and necessary to be vsed and said of al ttue [sic] English men, in these daungerous daies of affliction, for the com

text: Be not alwayes wroth at vs (O lord) but spare thi people, and haue mercye vpon thyne owne congregacion.
author: Bale, John, 1495-1563, attributed name.
title: An excellent and a right learned meditacion, compiled in two prayers most frutefull and necessary to be vsed and said of al ttue [sic] English men, in these daungerous daies of affliction, for the com

text: Plato verie wisely did thinke it a thing of greate importaunce, emong the customes of Citizens, to sette doune what maner of Musicke Citezens might vse.
author: Salter, Thomas.
title: A mirrhor mete for all mothers, matrones, and maidens, intituled the Mirrhor of Modestie no lesse profitable and pleasant, then necessarie to bee read and practiced.

text: Alas what should I saie will they alwaies be busied aboute suche nedelesse businesse? and neuer espie tyme and leisure to preferre my sute?
author: Salter, Thomas.
title: A mirrhor mete for all mothers, matrones, and maidens, intituled the Mirrhor of Modestie no lesse profitable and pleasant, then necessarie to bee read and practiced.

text: THE Goddesse Uertue hath praied me by her Letters, to make my presente repaire vnto her: whereto I willynly accorde, onely to vnderstande her pleasure, that ended, I muste make spedie retourne toward Iupiter.
author: Salter, Thomas.
title: A mirrhor mete for all mothers, matrones, and maidens, intituled the Mirrhor of Modestie no lesse profitable and pleasant, then necessarie to bee read and practiced.

text: But especially being in the companie of graue and wise women, I wishe her to be attentiue to heare that whiche they saie, and she not to speake to oftē, for as she that speaketh often is in danger to faile.
author: Salter, Thomas.
title: A mirrhor mete for all mothers, matrones, and maidens, intituled the Mirrhor of Modestie no lesse profitable and pleasant, then necessarie to bee read and practiced.

text: But my intent is not, neither was it euer, to attribute suche euill as springeth from the mallice of wicked men, and their corrupte nature, to the sacred studie of learnyng, to whiche I haue giuen my mynde so muche as in me laye all my life tyme.
author: Salter, Thomas.
title: A mirrhor mete for all mothers, matrones, and maidens, intituled the Mirrhor of Modestie no lesse profitable and pleasant, then necessarie to bee read and practiced.

text: Besides I am not mynded (how bee it that we are bounde to bowe to our superiours) to bowe or bend vnto thee, least I should ronne thereby into dishonour and infamie.
author: Salter, Thomas.
title: A mirrhor mete for all mothers, matrones, and maidens, intituled the Mirrhor of Modestie no lesse profitable and pleasant, then necessarie to bee read and practiced.

text: To speake a truthe, I nothyng moued in deede at her commyng, neither did I, or any of my companie passe for her, wherefore she proceaded forthe, and proudely saied, why gentlewoman will you not sturre?
author: Salter, Thomas.
title: A mirrhor mete for all mothers, matrones, and maidens, intituled the Mirrhor of Modestie no lesse profitable and pleasant, then necessarie to bee read and practiced.

text: And therefore to the ende that in so gallant a race oure Maiden maie not see anie thing to hinder or staie her atchiuing to the ende.
author: Salter, Thomas.
title: A mirrhor mete for all mothers, matrones, and maidens, intituled the Mirrhor of Modestie no lesse profitable and pleasant, then necessarie to bee read and practiced.

text: The whiche as it ought not to bee desired viciously, so ought it not to be refused with too great an opinion of vertue.
author: Salter, Thomas.
title: A mirrhor mete for all mothers, matrones, and maidens, intituled the Mirrhor of Modestie no lesse profitable and pleasant, then necessarie to bee read and practiced.

text: And gaue the Onſet to the fleſh, and conquered hath the ſame: As Champian bould, by Shield of Faith, to glorie of his name.
author: Bourman, Nicholas.
title: An epytaphe vpon the death of the Right worshipfull, Sir william Garrat Knight: and chiefe alderman of the Queenes Maiesties Citie of London Who deceased the. 27. of September. 1571. anno aetatis sue.

text: Since fatall Doome hath pluckt frō them ſo ſage & wiſe a Knight What double loſſe hath Ladie his? (that vertuous Matron graue,) Whom God had linckt to him as Spouſe, for terme of lyfe to haue.
author: Bourman, Nicholas.
title: An epytaphe vpon the death of the Right worshipfull, Sir william Garrat Knight: and chiefe alderman of the Queenes Maiesties Citie of London Who deceased the. 27. of September. 1571. anno aetatis sue.

text: Graunt this O God eternally, that when this race is ronne: Their Worſhips may obtain the Fame that GARRAT hath begon.
author: Bourman, Nicholas.
title: An epytaphe vpon the death of the Right worshipfull, Sir william Garrat Knight: and chiefe alderman of the Queenes Maiesties Citie of London Who deceased the. 27. of September. 1571. anno aetatis sue.

text: In Godlines, or ſacred lyfe, his ſteppes, the Lorde hath bleſt: whoſe endleſſe Fame reuiueth ſtill, though Corps be now ſuppreſt By Natures courſe.
author: Bourman, Nicholas.
title: An epytaphe vpon the death of the Right worshipfull, Sir william Garrat Knight: and chiefe alderman of the Queenes Maiesties Citie of London Who deceased the. 27. of September. 1571. anno aetatis sue.

text: A Patron of his Countrey deare intombde he hath, to name: For as the Senate graunts him right, the Cōmons ſay the ſame.
author: Bourman, Nicholas.
title: An epytaphe vpon the death of the Right worshipfull, Sir william Garrat Knight: and chiefe alderman of the Queenes Maiesties Citie of London Who deceased the. 27. of September. 1571. anno aetatis sue.

text: Whiche full Effect conſidered well, as Flowers in the Field: we may conceiue this outwarde man, in tract of time ſhall yeld, And hange the head: for as the ſhade that glydeth on the wall, compared with the Lillie faire, ſo ſodaine is our fall.
author: Bourman, Nicholas.
title: An epytaphe vpon the death of the Right worshipfull, Sir william Garrat Knight: and chiefe alderman of the Queenes Maiesties Citie of London Who deceased the. 27. of September. 1571. anno aetatis sue.

text: What rufull loſſe hath all the ſtate, of Senatours degree? with whome for Counſaile graue, he was accepted wont to bee.
author: Bourman, Nicholas.
title: An epytaphe vpon the death of the Right worshipfull, Sir william Garrat Knight: and chiefe alderman of the Queenes Maiesties Citie of London Who deceased the. 27. of September. 1571. anno aetatis sue.

text: What loſſe hath Children deare, of him? what loſſe hath ſeruants al? what loſſe hath eche that flood in neede, for Counſell his to call?
author: Bourman, Nicholas.
title: An epytaphe vpon the death of the Right worshipfull, Sir william Garrat Knight: and chiefe alderman of the Queenes Maiesties Citie of London Who deceased the. 27. of September. 1571. anno aetatis sue.

text: There is not one, that can reproue, one Title of his right, But as he was, (euen ſo he died:) to lyue a faithfull Knight.
author: Bourman, Nicholas.
title: An epytaphe vpon the death of the Right worshipfull, Sir william Garrat Knight: and chiefe alderman of the Queenes Maiesties Citie of London Who deceased the. 27. of September. 1571. anno aetatis sue.

text: For if yu go about to pleaſe any other, hee forſaketh thee and ioyneth him ſelf to other yūg ones.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo, attributed name.
title: A little pamphlet entituled the ladder of paradise Very worthy and needful to be read of every Christian that is willing to tread the steps which lead to heauen.

text: For it had béene better for them whome ſuch cauſe pulleth away from their holy purpoſe, not to knowe the glory of God then to tourn backwarde after they haue knowne it.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo, attributed name.
title: A little pamphlet entituled the ladder of paradise Very worthy and needful to be read of every Christian that is willing to tread the steps which lead to heauen.

text: O Lord how dooſt thou appéer when thou woorkeſt theſe thinge? & what token is ther of thy comming?
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo, attributed name.
title: A little pamphlet entituled the ladder of paradise Very worthy and needful to be read of every Christian that is willing to tread the steps which lead to heauen.

text: For that wiſdome, humain ſtudy of learning (but not the ſpirite of wiſdome) had giuen them, which ſpirite onely giueth true wiſdome, I mean the ſwéet knowledge, whiche when it is in any man as an ineſtimable ſwéetnes, it dooth comfort & refreſh him.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo, attributed name.
title: A little pamphlet entituled the ladder of paradise Very worthy and needful to be read of every Christian that is willing to tread the steps which lead to heauen.

text: Whilſt thou Lord dooſt break vnto me the bread of holy Scripture, & in breaking of bread: thou art the ſooner knowen, & the more I knowe thée: ye more I deſire to knowe thée, not now in the bark of the letter: but in the féeling of experience.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo, attributed name.
title: A little pamphlet entituled the ladder of paradise Very worthy and needful to be read of every Christian that is willing to tread the steps which lead to heauen.

text: If it be ſo ſweet a thing to weep for thee: how ſweet ſhall it be to reioyce of thee?
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo, attributed name.
title: A little pamphlet entituled the ladder of paradise Very worthy and needful to be read of every Christian that is willing to tread the steps which lead to heauen.

text: And therfore Saint Iohn vvriteth one of his epiſtles vnto a Lady, that Ladies alſo hauing the vvoord of God ſo eſpecially dyrected vnto them, might endeuour thēſelues vvith the greter dyligēce to read it and certēly knovv themſelues not to be excluded frō the exerciſe therof.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo, attributed name.
title: A little pamphlet entituled the ladder of paradise Very worthy and needful to be read of every Christian that is willing to tread the steps which lead to heauen.

text: Dooſt thou not ſée what abundance of licour hath flowed out of a litle Grape? how great a fire is growen out of this one ſpark? how far this litle lamp (Bleſſed are the pure in hart for they shall ſee God) is ſtretched out in this meditation.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo, attributed name.
title: A little pamphlet entituled the ladder of paradise Very worthy and needful to be read of every Christian that is willing to tread the steps which lead to heauen.

text: The very nāe of Gods vvoord ought to ſtrike into our harts, great reuerēce tovvard it, great deſire to haue it, great haſte to hear it, great loue to read it & like care to keep it.
author: Augustine, Saint, Bishop of Hippo, attributed name.
title: A little pamphlet entituled the ladder of paradise Very worthy and needful to be read of every Christian that is willing to tread the steps which lead to heauen.

text: For the eie hath not ſéene, and the eare hath not heard, neither haue entred into any mans minde ye things that God hath prepared for them ye loue him.
author: Brooke, John, d. 1582.
title: A Christian discourse vpon certaine poynts of religion Presented vnto the most high puissant Lorde, the Prince of Conde. Translated out of French into English by Iohn Brooke of Ashe next Sandwich. 157

text: Secondly, he doth offende the Prince vnto whome he ought to yelde himſelfe ſubiect, as ſainct Paule ſaith, not onely for feare of vengeaunce: but alſo bycauſe of conſcience.
author: Brooke, John, d. 1582.
title: A Christian discourse vpon certaine poynts of religion Presented vnto the most high puissant Lorde, the Prince of Conde. Translated out of French into English by Iohn Brooke of Ashe next Sandwich. 157

text: Beholde the doctrine of Salomon, crying with a loude voyce, ſaying: My ſonne heare thy Fathers doctrine, and forſake not the lawe of thy Mother: For that ſhall bringe grace vnto thy head, and ſhall bee as a chayne aboute thy necke.
author: Brooke, John, d. 1582.
title: A Christian discourse vpon certaine poynts of religion Presented vnto the most high puissant Lorde, the Prince of Conde. Translated out of French into English by Iohn Brooke of Ashe next Sandwich. 157

text: Chriſt, loking for the hope of the bleſſed, & the comming of the ſonne of God, of the which the Apoſtle ſainct Paul ſpeaketh off, ſaying: forbeare one another through loue, endeuouring to kéepe the vnitie of the ſpirite in the bonde of peace.
author: Brooke, John, d. 1582.
title: A Christian discourse vpon certaine poynts of religion Presented vnto the most high puissant Lorde, the Prince of Conde. Translated out of French into English by Iohn Brooke of Ashe next Sandwich. 157

text: Of the whiche the wiſe man Salomon ſpeaking off, ſaith: It was neither herbe nor plaiſter, that reſtored thē to health, but thy worde (O Lorde) whiche healeth all thinges.
author: Brooke, John, d. 1582.
title: A Christian discourse vpon certaine poynts of religion Presented vnto the most high puissant Lorde, the Prince of Conde. Translated out of French into English by Iohn Brooke of Ashe next Sandwich. 157

text: Who hath made mannes mouth, or who hath made the dum or the deafe, the ſeing or ye blinde? haue not I ye Lord?
author: Brooke, John, d. 1582.
title: A Christian discourse vpon certaine poynts of religion Presented vnto the most high puissant Lorde, the Prince of Conde. Translated out of French into English by Iohn Brooke of Ashe next Sandwich. 157

text: All men doe knowe very well howe the kingdomes of Dauyd and Salomon his ſonne haue proſpered in reſpect of thoſe of Pharao, Saul and Nabuchodonoſor.
author: Brooke, John, d. 1582.
title: A Christian discourse vpon certaine poynts of religion Presented vnto the most high puissant Lorde, the Prince of Conde. Translated out of French into English by Iohn Brooke of Ashe next Sandwich. 157

text: Truely the vſe of the worde which conſiſteth chiefly in the conuerſion of a ſinner, ought to be referred to all thoſe which haue hope of the eternall life.
author: Brooke, John, d. 1582.
title: A Christian discourse vpon certaine poynts of religion Presented vnto the most high puissant Lorde, the Prince of Conde. Translated out of French into English by Iohn Brooke of Ashe next Sandwich. 157

text: O Lorde which haſt made faſt for euer and euer all thy commaundements, in all truth and equitie: and which putteſt in man both the will and the deſire to fulfill them.
author: Brooke, John, d. 1582.
title: A Christian discourse vpon certaine poynts of religion Presented vnto the most high puissant Lorde, the Prince of Conde. Translated out of French into English by Iohn Brooke of Ashe next Sandwich. 157

text: They which come of our dyet, are called Sporadici: and by our breathing are engendred Endemij, and Epidemii.
author: Drouet, Pierre, fl. 1578.
title: A new counsell against the pestilence declaring what kinde of disease it is, of what cause it procedeth, the signes and tokens thereof: with the order of curing the same.

text: If there appeare any ſwelling in the necke, or about the eares, or any other ſignes declare the infection to bée in the Braine, the forehead veine muſt be opened, or elſe the ſmall veines in the Noſe, with Milfoile thruſt into the noſtrels, or with ſome other pricking thing.
author: Drouet, Pierre, fl. 1578.
title: A new counsell against the pestilence declaring what kinde of disease it is, of what cause it procedeth, the signes and tokens thereof: with the order of curing the same.

author: Underdown, Thomas.

author: Underdown, Thomas.

author: Underdown, Thomas.

text: Alſo hee muſt ſuffre her Ryotes: for a faire woman wyll, that none but ſhee haue her commaundementes in the Howſe.

text: So difficulte a woorke it is to discourse, the liues bothe of the good and bad, as (according to Senicaes opinion) it is ncessarie that the vertuous reporte the one, and the vitious publishe the other.

text: VVhen their sweete liues, at large for to recight, VVhiche liu'de, belou'de, and blameles scapeth deede Maks men doe well, on zeale & not through dreede.
author: Whetstone, George, 1544?-1587?

text: The wrathfull man, is sildome free from woe, A prouerbe olde, but daiely proued true, The eger Cocke, this furie right doeth showe, The whiche till death, doeth still his fight pursue.
author: Whetstone, George, 1544?-1587?

text: Let Cesars faule (that laied the world a longe) Fore warne hie mindes how thei with Enuie swell, VVormes profer force, against vnkindly wronge, Then man, that beares, of creatures all the bell.
author: Whetstone, George, 1544?-1587?

text: The like of lust, with loue it lulls the fleashe, Till from the bones, it doeth the marrowe threashe.
author: Whetstone, George, 1544?-1587?

text: These godlie woordes, in greatest griefes he vsde VVhiche daiely he, in vertuous woorkes did proue And in this mynde (whose might, but fewe abusde) VVith euery man, in charitie and loue, VVhom deadly panges, to passions could not moue.
author: Whetstone, George, 1544?-1587?
title: A remembraunce, of the woorthie and well imployed life, of the right honorable Sir Nicholas Bacon Knight, Lorde keper of the greate Seale of Englande, and one of the Queenes Maiesties most honorable P

text: Euen one of those, sir Nicholas Bacon was, Lorde keeper late, keye of the common weale, VVhose death his ioye, makes many sithe alas, Her Maiestie, who knewe his faithfull zeale, Her Counsell, when, in greate affaires thei deale.
author: Whetstone, George, 1544?-1587?
title: A remembraunce, of the woorthie and well imployed life, of the right honorable Sir Nicholas Bacon Knight, Lorde keper of the greate Seale of Englande, and one of the Queenes Maiesties most honorable P

text: The Prouerbe goeth, once olde, againe a page, But till he died, his graue aduise did deale, In woorkes of worthe, vnto the common weale.
author: Whetstone, George, 1544?-1587?

text: Beſides, what profeſſion of honour make you, in embaſing ſo much your minde, as hauing practiſed onely one Gentlewoman, you dare not aduenture vpon a higher enterpriſe.
author: Pasquier, Etienne, 1529-1615.
title: Monophylo, Drawne into English by Geffray Fenton. A philosophicall discourse, and diuision of loue

text: But beware of the ſtorme that ſuccéedes the flickering calme, and (with the wiſe Arthitecture) when you prepare a plot to buyld vpon, be ſure to ſée in your mind the toppe of your pallayce, afore you pitch your foundation.
author: Pasquier, Etienne, 1529-1615.
title: Monophylo, Drawne into English by Geffray Fenton. A philosophicall discourse, and diuision of loue

text: For as farre as I can gather of your contention (as one matter drawes on another) from loue ſimplie, (as you terme it) you are diſcended to maryage.
author: Pasquier, Etienne, 1529-1615.
title: Monophylo, Drawne into English by Geffray Fenton. A philosophicall discourse, and diuision of loue

text: And therfore ſéeing there is a diuerſity of fancie betwene you, let euery one féed on his priuate opinion without ſéeking to diſenherite his companion.
author: Pasquier, Etienne, 1529-1615.
title: Monophylo, Drawne into English by Geffray Fenton. A philosophicall discourse, and diuision of loue

text: And in a little glaunce of hir eye is harbored ſuch power (with the nature of the Baſilike) to pearce you, that blaſted with that inchauntment, you ſéeke to die afore your tyme.
author: Pasquier, Etienne, 1529-1615.
title: Monophylo, Drawne into English by Geffray Fenton. A philosophicall discourse, and diuision of loue

text: Oh Madame (ſayth he) God defend that my mouth ſhould deliuer ſuch ſpeach: yea, if I were guiltie but in thought, I woulde reſtore the fault with criminall penance, and laying my ſelfe vpon the ſentence of all Ladyes, I would endure mortall puniſhment as a mylde iuſtice.
author: Pasquier, Etienne, 1529-1615.
title: Monophylo, Drawne into English by Geffray Fenton. A philosophicall discourse, and diuision of loue

text: And ſo where afore there was a ſympathia and concordaunce of friendſhip, both the one and other are now tranſlated into lothſome ſpirites, ſtryuing eyther of them to maintaine and poſſeſſe their right.
author: Pasquier, Etienne, 1529-1615.
title: Monophylo, Drawne into English by Geffray Fenton. A philosophicall discourse, and diuision of loue

text: And for your eſtate pollitike, I praye you of what dependes this humaine felowſhip, which we haue named mutuall entertainment, if not of a reciprocall friendſhippe which we ought to beare one to another, the ſame being defaced by this wicked inuention of dowries.
author: Pasquier, Etienne, 1529-1615.
title: Monophylo, Drawne into English by Geffray Fenton. A philosophicall discourse, and diuision of loue

text: In loue (ſeigneur Monophylo) you maintaine a coniunction of one to one, without enforcing the dutie by which we are bounde to our myſtreſſes.
author: Pasquier, Etienne, 1529-1615.
title: Monophylo, Drawne into English by Geffray Fenton. A philosophicall discourse, and diuision of loue

text: Forbidding moſte expreſſely all our ſaied ſubiects, to reproche them with any matter that is paſt: forbiddinge alſo all our Iudges and Officers to trouble them, or to moleſt them, either in their perſonnes, or in their goodes.

text: Then do I pray him make discourse of Caesars triumphes braue, And eke what vowes that duty driu'th, the Latian Ioue to haue.
author: Ovid, 43 B.C.-17 or 18 A.D.
title: The three first bookes of Ouid de Tristibus translated into English

text: In barbarous Land I liu, and Pontus Isle hath mee possest, The Archadian Beare hath me also, and Boreas wynde distrest.
author: Ovid, 43 B.C.-17 or 18 A.D.
title: The three first bookes of Ouid de Tristibus translated into English

text: And faythfull breast with wayghty strokes, wil strike with feareful hād And hytherwardes in vayne although, thy wofull armes stretch out?
author: Ovid, 43 B.C.-17 or 18 A.D.
title: The three first bookes of Ouid de Tristibus translated into English

text: And though thou there a straunger be, thinke not vnknowen to come But that amids the mighty towne thou shalt be knowen to some.
author: Ovid, 43 B.C.-17 or 18 A.D.
title: The three first bookes of Ouid de Tristibus translated into English

text: But madnes now with feuer fearce, are ioyned so in one, That mindfull yet of former payne, my foote doth strike the stone.
author: Ovid, 43 B.C.-17 or 18 A.D.
title: The three first bookes of Ouid de Tristibus translated into English

text: The floods my mind opprest while thus, in vaine we prayd alas, And by our carefull mouth adowne, the deadly drops do pas.
author: Ovid, 43 B.C.-17 or 18 A.D.
title: The three first bookes of Ouid de Tristibus translated into English

text: These happy signes most comely be, that pleasaunt Poets were, My troublous time is farre vnfit the Lawrell crowne to beare.
author: Ovid, 43 B.C.-17 or 18 A.D.
title: The three first bookes of Ouid de Tristibus translated into English

text: Thou knowst to whom I speake although thy name in sygnes I set, Thy duty and thy frendly care, no whit I do forget.
author: Ovid, 43 B.C.-17 or 18 A.D.
title: The three first bookes of Ouid de Tristibus translated into English

text: No learned mates for conference, do liue within this lande, That hath the skill my verse to reade, or eares to vnderstande.
author: Ovid, 43 B.C.-17 or 18 A.D.
title: The three first bookes of Ouid de Tristibus translated into English

text: O woorke mine harte a newe, after thine accuſtomed manner, and according to thy good promiſſes of olde.
author: Palfreyman, Thomas, d. 1589?
title: [Divine meditations.]

text: How ſhould we (moſte ſinnefull wretches) in theſe dayes, abide the terror of thy vengeance, that by thy iuſtice hangeth ouer vs, or ſhould in a moment conſume vs all like ſtubble.
author: Palfreyman, Thomas, d. 1589?
title: [Divine meditations.]

text: Thine exaltation vppon the croſſe (O Lord) hath bene (as I beleeue) long ſince perfourmed, as alſo thy riſing againe from deathe, and thine aftention into heauen.
author: Palfreyman, Thomas, d. 1589?
title: [Divine meditations.]

text: O what a happines therfore is it to a mā, to caſt fréely frō him, al impedimēts & lettes of worldly vanities, & yéelde him ſelf wholely vnder thine hand of diſcipline, and to the chaſtening of his ſoule.
author: Palfreyman, Thomas, d. 1589?
title: [Divine meditations.]

text: Yea, and I know aſſuredly, that throgh thy goodneſſe and feruent charitie, thou act inforced to vanquiſhe and vtterly ouerthrow my weakeneſſe, wickeoneſſe, malice and blindneſſe, euen to the pardoning of all (from the firſte to the laſte) that hathe beene amiſſe.
author: Palfreyman, Thomas, d. 1589?
title: [Divine meditations.]

text: No no Lorde, thou haſt treaſures yet ſuperfluous, which ſhal endure for euer: and wilt not thou aide and comforte me thy poore & wretched creature with the crums that fall from thy table, for my moſt ioyful refection ſeeing me now in danger & irke to periſh?
author: Palfreyman, Thomas, d. 1589?
title: [Divine meditations.]

text: I may yet eſcape the fulneſſe of thy paimēt due for euer to the wicked, by theyr deadly and iuſte deſerte.
author: Palfreyman, Thomas, d. 1589?
title: [Divine meditations.]

text: Al thy diuine treaſures are mine: yea, and euen thou thy ſelfe art wholely alſo mine, Thy father hath giuen thée vnto me, and thou alſo was contented that I ſhould poſſeſſe thée, and therfore thou canſt not nowe denie thy ſelfe to be mine.
author: Palfreyman, Thomas, d. 1589?
title: [Divine meditations.]

text: And haſt thou not ſpent, euen thy moſte precious heart bloud for me, ſuffering for my ſake, ſo many & ſo extreame paines & moſte greeuous torments?
author: Palfreyman, Thomas, d. 1589?
title: [Divine meditations.]

text: ANd in the.ix. daye of the Moone, Lameth was borne, to do all thynges it is profytable, what thyng thou wylte entre to make, it is good, and ſhall profyte.
author: Godfridus.
title: Here begynneth the boke of knowledge of thynges vnknowen aperteynynge to astronomye with certayne necessarye rules, and certayne speres contaynyng herein compyled by Godfridus super Palladum de agricu

text: And nexte after that reygneth the Planette that is nexte in ordre as thus Saturne, Iupiter, Mars, Sol, Venus Mercurius and Luna.
author: Godfridus.
title: Here begynneth the boke of knowledge of thynges vnknowen aperteynynge to astronomye with certayne necessarye rules, and certayne speres contaynyng herein compyled by Godfridus super Palladum de agricu

text: A mayden childe than borne, ſhalbe eyght ſycke: ſaue not payde of one man, that daye is good to blede.
author: Godfridus.
title: Here begynneth the boke of knowledge of thynges vnknowen aperteynynge to astronomye with certayne necessarye rules, and certayne speres contaynyng herein compyled by Godfridus super Palladum de agricu

text: On ſaturdaye the fyrſte howre after mydnyght, reygneth Saturne, the ſeconde howre Iupiter, the thyrde howre Mars, the.iiij. howre Sol, the.v. howre Venus, the.vi. howre Mercurie, the.vij. howre, Luna.
author: Godfridus.
title: Here begynneth the boke of knowledge of thynges vnknowen aperteynynge to astronomye with certayne necessarye rules, and certayne speres contaynyng herein compyled by Godfridus super Palladum de agricu

text: A dreme within ſyxe dayes ſhalbe, to make weddynge it is good, and to go in the waye.
author: Godfridus.
title: Here begynneth the boke of knowledge of thynges vnknowen aperteynynge to astronomye with certayne necessarye rules, and certayne speres contaynyng herein compyled by Godfridus super Palladum de agricu

text: A man that falleth ſycke, eyther ſoone ſhalbe healed, or ſoone ſhal dye, it is good to let blod.
author: Godfridus.
title: Here begynneth the boke of knowledge of thynges vnknowen aperteynynge to astronomye with certayne necessarye rules, and certayne speres contaynyng herein compyled by Godfridus super Palladum de agricu

text: Thondre ī Septembre, ſygnyfyeth that ſame yere great wynde copye of corne, that is to ſaye, plenteous, and occaſyon of folke, that is to ſay, moch fallynge.
author: Godfridus.
title: Here begynneth the boke of knowledge of thynges vnknowen aperteynynge to astronomye with certayne necessarye rules, and certayne speres contaynyng herein compyled by Godfridus super Palladum de agricu

text: Who that waxeth ſycke, longe tyme ſhall trauayle, and vnneth ſhall be ſaued but dye: Towed a wyfe, it is good, it is good eche daye to let blode.
author: Godfridus.
title: Here begynneth the boke of knowledge of thynges vnknowen aperteynynge to astronomye with certayne necessarye rules, and certayne speres contaynyng herein compyled by Godfridus super Palladum de agricu

text: A ſycke man that falleth in his bed, ſhal trauayle, and he ſhal not ſcape, to let blode it is good.
author: Godfridus.

text: Of this there hath beene made many trialls, and in London, it was first assaide by Master Westwood a refiner dwelling in woodstreet, and it helde after the rate of 12000 or 13000 pounds a tunne.
author: Raleigh, Walter, Sir, 1552?-1618.

text: And where the south border of Guiana reacheth to the Dominion and Empire of the Amazones, those women shall heereby heare the name of a virgin, which is not onely able to defend her owne territories and her neighbors, but also to inuade and conquere so great Empyres and so farre remoued.
author: Raleigh, Walter, Sir, 1552?-1618.

author: Smith, Richard, 1500-1563.

author: Smith, Richard, 1500-1563.
title: A brief treatyse settynge forth diuers truthes necessary both to be beleued of Chrysten people, kepte also, whiche are not expressed in the Scripture but left to ye church by the apostles traditio[n]

text: Then why do we thruſte (ſayeth Vrbanus regius wiſely) in ye churches hādes ye lawes of men, as neceſſary to chriſtes religion?
author: Smith, Richard, 1500-1563.

text: From thence it is open, that the apoſtles dyd not teach all thynges by an epiſtle, but alſo many thinges with our wrytynge.

text: Keepe thou (O good Lorde) her highnes from the murmuring of Dathan, Coran, and Abiram, which enuie the godly eſtate of her gouernment, and let theyr reward bee ſhame and confuſion, which imagine to worke her highnes any harme.
author: I. P.
title: A godlie and zealous prayer to bee vsed of euery Christian and duetifull [sic] subiecte for the preseruation of our most soueraigne Lady Elizabeth, by the grace of God, of England, Fraunce, and Irelan

text: Make them of perſecuting Saules, to become conuerted Paules, that they with vs, and we with them, may glory and triumphe in the fall of Babilon, and ſtudie in all theyr and our actions, as it becommeth redeemed Chriſtians to aduaunce and ſet foorth the glory of thy holy name.
author: I. P.
title: A godlie and zealous prayer to bee vsed of euery Christian and duetifull [sic] subiecte for the preseruation of our most soueraigne Lady Elizabeth, by the grace of God, of England, Fraunce, and Irelan

text: Keepe her farre off good Lord we beſeeche thee, from all ſuch ambitious minded Abſolons, as haue determined to alter the eſtate of her moſt gracious gouernment, and let their hire be ſhame and confuſion that haue conſpired againſt her and thy people.
author: I. P.
title: A godlie and zealous prayer to bee vsed of euery Christian and duetifull [sic] subiecte for the preseruation of our most soueraigne Lady Elizabeth, by the grace of God, of England, Fraunce, and Irelan

text: And then thou like a louing father and moſt gracious God, wilt mercifully ſtretch foorth vnto vs the aſſured Scepter of thy euerlaſting fauour: double the dayes of our ſoueraigne, to our exceeding ioy and comfort.
author: I. P.
title: A godlie and zealous prayer to bee vsed of euery Christian and duetifull [sic] subiecte for the preseruation of our most soueraigne Lady Elizabeth, by the grace of God, of England, Fraunce, and Irelan

text: Increaſe the number of godly Subiects, and giue vs grace we beſeeche thee O eternall God, truely to ſerue and worſhippe thee, to hate ſinne, to flye farre from the fellowſhip of the vngodly, and to abound in all obedience, loue and duety towardes thee and her maieſty.
author: I. P.
title: A godlie and zealous prayer to bee vsed of euery Christian and duetifull [sic] subiecte for the preseruation of our most soueraigne Lady Elizabeth, by the grace of God, of England, Fraunce, and Irelan

text: Stretch foorth thy hand O heauenly Father, and euer defend thy handmayd from thoſe deuouring Bulles of Baſan, which haue bent their hornes againſt her, hardning their hartes in their vngodlines, to worke the confuſion of ſo vertuous and godly a Princeſſe.
author: I. P.
title: A godlie and zealous prayer to bee vsed of euery Christian and duetifull [sic] subiecte for the preseruation of our most soueraigne Lady Elizabeth, by the grace of God, of England, Fraunce, and Irelan

text: Vpholde we beſeeche thee amongſt vs, as graciouſly thou haſt doone hetherto, the ſincere preaching of thy Goſpell, (O moſt mighty Iehoua) and giue vs grace without wauering, to hold faſt the ſtaffe of thy bleſſed promiſes, and to beleeue without faining the ſacred teſtimonies contained in thy holy Lawe.
author: I. P.
title: A godlie and zealous prayer to bee vsed of euery Christian and duetifull [sic] subiecte for the preseruation of our most soueraigne Lady Elizabeth, by the grace of God, of England, Fraunce, and Irelan

text: And cheefely and eſpecially, (O gracious God and louing father) we commende vnto thee in theſe our prayers and ſupplications at this preſent, according to our bounden dueties, the eſtate of thy choſen ſeruaunt, our ſoueraigne Lady, Queene Elizabeth.
author: I. P.
title: A godlie and zealous prayer to bee vsed of euery Christian and duetifull [sic] subiecte for the preseruation of our most soueraigne Lady Elizabeth, by the grace of God, of England, Fraunce, and Irelan

text: Ieſus Chriſt was contented to ride on an Aſſe, the Apoſtles thought it no ſkorne to goe barefoote: and we embrace gladlye, with reuerence their patience, humilitie, vertue, and mild manner in planting the Goſpel.
author: Frarinus, Petrus.
title: An oration against the vnlawfull insurrections of the protestantes of our time, vnder pretence to refourme religion Made and pronounced in Latin, in the Schole of Artes at Louaine, the .xiij. of Decem

text: For what one mā of you all (right honorable & worſhipfull) wold gladly or willingly allow and beare ſuche & ſo hainous enormities in any Realme or Country?
author: Frarinus, Petrus.

text: For the perſons and holy Sayntes of God, againſt whome all this crueltie and extremitie of malice is ſhewed, be all one, of the ſame Catholike fayth and Religion, and much about the ſame age and tyme, far within ſyxe hundred yeres after Chriſte.
author: Frarinus, Petrus.

text: Therefore, I ſaye vnto you of al theſe, beware, and take héede that you be not ſeduced, and ſettle your conſciences vpon that ſure foundation and ſtronge rocke of Chriſtes Goſpell whereof before I haue tolde you.

text: For heauen and earth ſhall periſhe and paſſe away in vanitie, but the worde of God ſhall not periſh, but that euery iote thereof ſhal be perfourmed.

text: But it becomes not me, perhaps, to tell you gods your dutie, yet thus much without offence, I hope, I may ſay, ſaying it truly: that the God of heauen is angrie with the gods on earth for want of dutie.

text: And in the hearing of the word, take we heede how wee heare: for then by little and by little the diuell will robbe vs of al, or fill our heads with so many toyes and by-matters, that we shall bee neuer the better, but the worse.

text: The matter of these verses is in generall a disswasion from idlenes and negligence: Idlenes for want of a calling, and negligence in a mans calling are the principall things which the spirite of God here dealeth against, perswading also to faithfull diligence, by the example of a sillie creature the Pismire.
author: Burton, William, d. 1616.

text: What is the reason that no man trauaileth in seeking out the cause of so monsterous a ruine: but that the desperate wickednes of that nation doth openly crye out that the same was the cause thereof?

text: Had not Moses prayed for the Israelites, they had perished oftentimes in their sinnes: so if some did not pray for vs, (whom yet wee can as hardly abide, as they could abide Moses when they would haue stoned him) surelie wee had perished yet this time.

text: Therefore let none be so desperatly minded as to continue still his old course, as though there were no hope of grace at his returne.

text: And the like we finde at home in perfourming our spiritual exercises, whether it bee of prayer, or reading, or singing Psalmes, or instructing our families, though Gods spirite doth sometime touch vs, and awake vs, yet are we soone forgetfull, and sleepe creepeth on againe.

text: A yet of God thou wilte not ceaſſe Tyll I fyght in good earneſſe On my fayth I tell the true yf I fyghte thou wylte it rue All the dayes of thy lyfe.
title: The enterlude of youth

text: Now ſyr by this light That wolde I fayne ſe And I plight the ſo God me ſaue That a ſurer tolere thou ſhalt haue And becauſe gold colers be ſo good chepe Vnto the roper I ſhal ſpeke To make the one of a good price And that ſhalbe of warranty ſe.
title: The enterlude of youth

text: A backe felowes and giue me roume Or I ſhall make you to auoyde ſone I am goodlye of perſone I am pereles where euer I come My name is youth I tell the I floryſh as the vine tre Who may be likened vnto me In my youthe and Iolitye My hearre is royall and buſhed thicke.
title: The enterlude of youth

text: Ieſu that was borne of Mare milde From all euyll he vs ſhielde And ſende you grace to amende Or oure lyfe be at an ende For I tell you trewlye That ye lyue full wickedlye I pray God it amende.
title: The enterlude of youth

text: Lo ſyrs loke what I bringe Is not this a ioly ringinge By my trouth I trowe it be I will go wyt of charitie How ſayeſt thou maiſter charitie Dothe this geare pleaſe the.
title: The enterlude of youth

text: Ieſu that ſytteth in heauen ſo hye Saue all this faire companye Men and women that here be Amen, Amen for charitie.
title: The enterlude of youth

text: what ſhal it be whan thou ſhalt flyt For the wealth into the pyt Therfore of it be not to boolde Leaſt thou for think it whan ye art old Ye maye be lykened to a tre In youth floryſhyng with royallte And in age it is cut downe And to the fyre is throwne.
title: The enterlude of youth

text: No horeſon ſayſt thou ſo Holde him pride and let me go I ſhal fet a prayre of rynges That ſhall ſit to his ſhinnes And that euen a none.

text: His Prudence ſhines, when to preſerue vs thus, All humane wit his wiſdome doth conuince: His gracious bountie in our bounteous Prince.

text: People, leſſe ſetled then the ſliding ſand; More mutable then Proteus, or the Moone; Turn'd and return'd in turning of a hand, Like Euripus ebbe-flowing euery Noone.
author: Du Nesme, Jean.
title: The miracle of the peace in Fraunce Celebrated by the ghost of the diuine Du Bartas. / Translated, by Iosuah Sylvester.

text: Let Ceres dwell vpon thy deſart Plaine, Bacchus, and Diane, on thy hilles and groues, Pomona in gardens, Pan among thy droues, Secure all Roades, and ope all gates againe.
author: Du Nesme, Jean.
title: The miracle of the peace in Fraunce Celebrated by the ghost of the diuine Du Bartas. / Translated, by Iosuah Sylvester.

text: Who well would keepe ſo plentifull a portion, Muſt ſtabliſh firſt the heau'nly diſcipline; Then humane Lawes, reſtraining all extortion; And princely wealth with publick weale cōbine.
author: Du Nesme, Jean.
title: The miracle of the peace in Fraunce Celebrated by the ghost of the diuine Du Bartas. / Translated, by Iosuah Sylvester.

text: But come to counter-min 'gainſt ſecret treaſon, Or force the forces of a ſtranger foe, Alas, how ſhallow are we then in reaſon, How cold in courage, and in camping ſlow?
author: Du Nesme, Jean.
title: The miracle of the peace in Fraunce Celebrated by the ghost of the diuine Du Bartas. / Translated, by Iosuah Sylvester.

text: For though it ſeeme to breath now ſome what peart, Our ſinnes I feare will worke worſe after-claps, And there's moſt danger in are-relaps.
author: Du Nesme, Jean.
title: The miracle of the peace in Fraunce Celebrated by the ghost of the diuine Du Bartas. / Translated, by Iosuah Sylvester.

text: Who nill be ſubiects, ſhall be ſlaues in fine: Who Kings refuſe, ſhall haue a Tyrant Lord: Who are not moou'd with the mild rods diuine, Shall feele the furie of heau'ns venging ſword.
author: Du Nesme, Jean.
title: The miracle of the peace in Fraunce Celebrated by the ghost of the diuine Du Bartas. / Translated, by Iosuah Sylvester.

text: When I heare Porters prate of State-deſignes, And make all common, as in new-found Indes.
author: Du Nesme, Jean.

text: FRance, without cauſe thou dooſt complaine Againſt the League for wronging thee, Sh'hath made thee large amends againe With more than common vſurie.
author: Du Nesme, Jean.
title: The miracle of the peace in Fraunce Celebrated by the ghost of the diuine Du Bartas. / Translated, by Iosuah Sylvester.

text: O omnipotent trinitie, thou whych liuest art the beginning of life thou art the perfect fairenes, and the blessed delectation.
author: Tunstall, Cuthbert, 1474-1559.
title: Certaine godly and deuout prayers. Made in latin by the Reuerend father in God, Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of Durham, and translated into Englishe by Thomas Paynell, clerke

text: O Lorde Iesu Chryst, the which being god immortal, tokest vp on the a mortall body, to make vs lawes to lyue holely & vertuously.
author: Tunstall, Cuthbert, 1474-1559.
title: Certaine godly and deuout prayers. Made in latin by the Reuerend father in God, Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of Durham, and translated into Englishe by Thomas Paynell, clerke

text: BLessed be the hyghe and the incomprehē sible Trinitie, the father, ye sonne and the holy Ghost, god lord, and comforter, charitie, grace, and communication.
author: Tunstall, Cuthbert, 1474-1559.
title: Certaine godly and deuout prayers. Made in latin by the Reuerend father in God, Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of Durham, and translated into Englishe by Thomas Paynell, clerke

text: IESU, whych after the innumeramerable tormentes of thy bodye, hangyng verye wekely vpon the crosse, vouchesauedest to dye for vs, haue mercy vpon vs.
author: Tunstall, Cuthbert, 1474-1559.
title: Certaine godly and deuout prayers. Made in latin by the Reuerend father in God, Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of Durham, and translated into Englishe by Thomas Paynell, clerke

text: Be mercyfull vnto vs mortall wretches we besech the, and despise vs not geuē to sīne, inasmuch as we ar thy hand worke: but through thy infinite clemency, deliuer and kepe vs from all euyl, & from all synne.
author: Tunstall, Cuthbert, 1474-1559.
title: Certaine godly and deuout prayers. Made in latin by the Reuerend father in God, Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of Durham, and translated into Englishe by Thomas Paynell, clerke

text: And inasmuche as we are not able to doo worthye penaunce for oure sinnes, nor satisfye the: set the crosse and the death, the paynes and the anguyshes, whiche thy onelye and welbeloued sonne our Lord Iesus Christ, an innocente, suffered mekely in this lyfe, for the abolyshment of our synnes.
author: Tunstall, Cuthbert, 1474-1559.
title: Certaine godly and deuout prayers. Made in latin by the Reuerend father in God, Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of Durham, and translated into Englishe by Thomas Paynell, clerke

text: Therfore O honorable Trynitie, all the citezens of heuen, patriarches, prophetes Apostles, martirs cōfessors and virgynes, shall glorifye thy maiestie.
author: Tunstall, Cuthbert, 1474-1559.
title: Certaine godly and deuout prayers. Made in latin by the Reuerend father in God, Cuthbert Tunstall, Bishop of Durham, and translated into Englishe by Thomas Paynell, clerke

text: O mercyfull Trinitie, we humble offer vp vnto ye, oure prayers, for the lyuyng and the deade, vnto whō they maye be profitable: to thentent yu shalt wash & blurre out theyr fautes & remitte to these their paynes, & to them bothe conferre and geue thy grace and glory.

text: And I doe thereby ſolemnly binde my ſelfe to Chriſt, to keepe his commaundements (to my power) and to beleeue and truſt in his merits, death and paſsion, for my ſaluation.
author: Butterfield, Swithun, d. 1611.
title: The principles of the true Christian religion breifelie selected, out of manie good bookes. first reade: and then iudge.

text: This petition teacheth vs to acknowledge our ſinnes, and as earneſtly as we may, To deſire of God forgiueneſſe of them: truſting in his mercie, for the merits, death, and paſsion of Chriſt Ieſus our Sauiour and redemer.
author: Butterfield, Swithun, d. 1611.
title: The principles of the true Christian religion breifelie selected, out of manie good bookes. first reade: and then iudge.

text: This definition being thus ſet downe, I come to that which you haue ſaide before, and I will firſt proue (if God ſhall aſſiſt mee) that dauncing is no recreation of the bodie, ſecondely that it is no recreation of the minde.
author: Fetherston, Christopher.
title: A dialogue agaynst light, lewde, and lasciuious dauncing wherin are refuted all those reasons, which the common people vse to bring in defence thereof. Compiled and made by Christopher Fetherston.

text: Therefore moſt fonde, fooliſh, and fantaſticall is the opinion of thoſe men, which doe thinke that dauncing was the onely thing whereby they came by their wyues.
author: Fetherston, Christopher.
title: A dialogue agaynst light, lewde, and lasciuious dauncing wherin are refuted all those reasons, which the common people vse to bring in defence thereof. Compiled and made by Christopher Fetherston.

text: Our ſinnes are many in number; & great are our iniquities, & our offences are gone ouer our heads, and are become a burthē to. heauy for vs to beare.
author: Fetherston, Christopher.
title: A dialogue agaynst light, lewde, and lasciuious dauncing wherin are refuted all those reasons, which the common people vse to bring in defence thereof. Compiled and made by Christopher Fetherston.

text: To whom ſhall the ſeruant, who hath eſpied weedes in the fieldes complayne, if not to the maiſter whoſe the fielde is?
author: Fetherston, Christopher.
title: A dialogue agaynst light, lewde, and lasciuious dauncing wherin are refuted all those reasons, which the common people vse to bring in defence thereof. Compiled and made by Christopher Fetherston.

text: Tuſhe tuſhe, wee will haue our ſwindg while we be yong, age wil come ſoone ynough, and it will make vs forſake all theſe ſportes: and then will wee be ſober and vertuous.
author: Fetherston, Christopher.
title: A dialogue agaynst light, lewde, and lasciuious dauncing wherin are refuted all those reasons, which the common people vse to bring in defence thereof. Compiled and made by Christopher Fetherston.

text: The cowleſtaffe ſtandeth in the corner, therefore the Pope is at Rome: my dagger hangeth at my backe, therefore my ſtaffe is in my hande.
author: Fetherston, Christopher.
title: A dialogue agaynst light, lewde, and lasciuious dauncing wherin are refuted all those reasons, which the common people vse to bring in defence thereof. Compiled and made by Christopher Fetherston.

text: Uppon which wordes, Chryſoſtome in his oration againſt the Iewes, ſayeth thus: Of a trueth, that whiche is done according to the will of God, although it ſeeme diſpleaſant: yet is it altogether pleaſant and acceptable in the ſyght of God.
author: Fetherston, Christopher.
title: A dialogue agaynst light, lewde, and lasciuious dauncing wherin are refuted all those reasons, which the common people vse to bring in defence thereof. Compiled and made by Christopher Fetherston.

text: I pray you, is the abſenting of menſelues from dauncing, the cauſe of theft and who oredome, or is that ſame naturall corruption, which raineth moſt chiefly in the heartes of thoſe whiche are moſt ſet vppon dauncing, the cauſe thereof?
author: Fetherston, Christopher.
title: A dialogue agaynst light, lewde, and lasciuious dauncing wherin are refuted all those reasons, which the common people vse to bring in defence thereof. Compiled and made by Christopher Fetherston.

text: For by this did they debarre the ſimple people from reading the woorde, whereby it came to paſſe that they could neuer eſpy out their iuglinge.

text: Corhinthians. iii. euen so is hys kyngdome spirituall inwardly within vs. Luke. xvii. and not of this worlde.

text: For we be leue and holy scrypture beareth wytnes, that Chryste after his resurrection is ascended vp into heauen, and sytteth vpon the ryght hand of his almighty father.

text: And of this couenauntes behalfe, whiche muste be done out of a cleane faythfull herte, hath the baptysme powre, and not for the waters sake, wherwith the fylthynesse of the fleshe myghte be washed awaye.

text: These wordes of Paule do witnesse clerely that the faythful eate the body of Christ spiritually, vnder the breade and wyne yea lykewyse as a bryde receyueth her housbande with a rynge, euen so receyue the faithfull Christe to be theyr owne and euerlastynge saluacyon.

text: Esay. liii. and hath taken awaye Sathans powre, and restored lyfe in agyne. i. Timot. vi. yea he is made vnto vs wysdome and ryghtwysnes, sanctyfyenge and redemption. i. Cor. i. And lykewyse as he dyed for our synnes.

text: Wyse and true counsell alas I dyd refuse Agayne reason vsyng my appetite Ambition did so my hert abuse That Eolus had me in great dispite Poetis of me hath mater to indyte Whylk clam so hye and wo is me therfore Not doubtyng that deth durst me deuore.

text: How in some court be barnes of Beliall Full of dissimuled paynted flattery Prouokynge by intoxicate counsall Princes to hooredome and tyll hasardry Who dothe in prynces prent syk harlotry I say for me suche pert prouocatours Sholde punissed be aboue all stronge traytours.

text: Among all other pastyme and pleasure Nowe in thy adolescent yeres yenge Wolde thou euery day study but half an houre The regiment of princely gouernynge To thy people it were a pleasaunt thynge Theyr myght thou fynd thy owne vocation How thou sholde vse thy scepture swerd and crown.

text: Whether I was stryken in extasy Or through a stark ymagination But it appereth in my fantasy I herd this dolent lamentation Thus dullid in to desolation Me thought this bird dyd discriue in hyr manere Her counssall to the king as ye shall here.

text: Request that roy whiche rent was on the roode The to defend frome dedes of defame That no poete report of the but good For princes dayes endures but a dreame Seyng fyrst kyng Fergus bare a diadeame Thou arte the last kynge of fiue score and fiue And all ar deed and none but thou on lyue.

text: Of thy vertue poetes perpetually Shall make mencyon vnto the worlde be ended So thou exercyse thy office prudently In heuen and erth thy grace shall be commended Wherfore beware that he be not offended Whilk has exalted the to sik honour Of this people to be a gouernour.

text: During his tyme so iustice did preuayle The sauage ylis trubled for terrour Eskdaile emsdaile liddisdaile and anuerdaile Durst not rebell doutyng his dintis dour And of his lordes had sik perfit sauour So forte shawe that he fered no fone Out through his realme he wold ride him alone.

text: Thus doo I ſée al hope of mās helpe taken from mee, and all comfort bereft mée: Wherefore I will henceforth ceaſe and bridle my deſires.
author: Galis, Richard.
title: [A brief treatise containing the most strange and horrible cruelty of Elizabeth Stile alias Rockingham and her confederates, executed at Abingdon, upon R. Galis]

text: Item that Mother Denel did ouer ſpeake one William Foſter a Fiſher, and one Hil his wife a Baker.

text: Nothing doubting, but that God knowing mine innocencie and the righteouſneſſe of my cauſe, would not onely proſper my attempt: but alſo giue me happy ſucceſſe to the ende of my trauayles.
author: Galis, Richard.
title: [A brief treatise containing the most strange and horrible cruelty of Elizabeth Stile alias Rockingham and her confederates, executed at Abingdon, upon R. Galis]

text: If I craue helpe of the inferior ſort (my correction ſo affrayes them) that albeit they would helpe, yet they dare not.

text: Wherfore I addreſſed my ſelf to the woorſhipfull Sir Henry Neuel Knight, who ſufficently before perſwaded of my troubles, and greatly with my good Lady his bedfellowe, (with whome I had often conference) pitying myne eſtate.
author: Galis, Richard.
title: [A brief treatise containing the most strange and horrible cruelty of Elizabeth Stile alias Rockingham and her confederates, executed at Abingdon, upon R. Galis]

text: At whom (my faith ſtedfaſtly ſet in the Lord) I let flye with my ſword, ſaying, auoide Sathan auoyde, and in the name of God I charge thée to auoide, thou haſt nought to do with mee, wherefore go hunte after the Doe which hath cauſed thée here to ſitte.
author: Galis, Richard.
